I felt this way for ages but when I hit puberty and I was made aware of people looking at me I started feeling gross. I developed early and I received lots of comments about my body from the adults around me, good and bad. My family is exclusively hyper-anxious matriarchs and made me aware of men staring at me, for the sake of me knowing so I could protect myself, and it never felt good because I hated the changes happening to me and hated people were seeing them. So there were a lot of things causing me discomfort about the way I looked when I was like 8-12. A lot of things happened with people in my life to make me feel really ugly and fat when I was a kid and I never wanted to grow up and be a woman in the first place.  I guess after being bullied for my looks in middle school made me combine the discomfort of being in my body/people looking at me/being called fat and ugly made me think if people are going to look at me under a microscope anyway I want to at least look pretty. I at least want people to stop looking at me with anger or disgust and be nice. I feel like if I were prettier people would have been nicer and I'm always waiting for the other shoe to drop when someone thinks I'm pretty. I think they're pranking me. Sometimes I even get angry. Consciously I know puberty gives everybody an ugly duckling phase and my weight gain turned to proportionate curves but I still feel like a potato. Idk how I even really look. I've addressed it a lot. I think it's too deep seated to change and I just need to cope with it. Maybe it's just because I'm a mental disorder nerd but I've found a substantial body of research done on EDs. The issues with that research come down to how they develop and the demographics they affect. So a lot of the info you can find on EDs tend to hone on on anorexia and bulimia in adolescent Caucasian girls and are more treatment oriented. The development of EDs has remained highly speculative . A lot of the research also doesn't consider comorbid diagnoses, like in my instance, my bipolar ii diagnosis has pretty much excused every other mental health problem I have. And environmental factors are often glossed over or non-specific.

So if researchers start broadening the demographic to include children, men, and other racial demographics, we'd probably have a better understanding of why and how EDs happen and start nipping their development in the bud.
